chunks.heading: What's inside an atom?
chunks.body: Every atom has a tiny, dense centre called the nucleus. A cloud of electrons surrounds it, taking up almost all of the atom's space.
chunks.checkText: Where are electrons found in an atom?

checkOptions.text: In a cloud around the nucleus

chunks.heading: Three particles, three charges
chunks.body: Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge, and electrons are negative. Electrons are so light that almost all of an atom's mass comes from its nucleus.
chunks.checkText: Which particle has no charge at all?

chunks.heading: The atomic number
chunks.body: The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. Every atom of the same element has the same atomic number.
chunks.checkText: The atomic number tells you the number of...

chunks.heading: The mass number
chunks.body: The mass number is the total count of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Subtract the [[chem-atomic-number|atomic number]] from it to find the number of neutrons.
chunks.checkText: To find the number of neutrons in an atom, you...

checkOptions.text: Subtract atomic number from mass number
Add atomic number to mass number

chunks.heading: Isotopes: same element, different mass
chunks.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same [[chem-atomic-number|atomic number]] but different [[chem-mass-number|mass numbers]]. They have different numbers of neutrons.
chunks.checkText: Isotopes of the same element always have the same number of...

chunks.heading: When isotopes are unstable
chunks.body: Some [[chem-isotopes|isotopes]] are unstable and are called radioisotopes. They break down over time, releasing radiation.
chunks.checkText: A radioisotope is an isotope that...

chunks.heading: Alpha radiation
chunks.body: An alpha particle is a heavy chunk made of two protons and two neutrons, released by unstable [[chem-radioisotopes|nuclei]]. It barely travels far and is stopped by a sheet of paper.
chunks.checkText: Alpha particles are stopped by...

chunks.heading: Beta radiation
chunks.body: A beta particle is a fast electron released when a neutron changes into a proton. It travels further than alpha radiation but is stopped by a thin sheet of metal.
chunks.checkText: A beta particle is actually a fast-moving...

chunks.heading: Gamma radiation
chunks.body: Gamma radiation is pure energy, not a particle. It travels the farthest of the three and needs thick lead to stop it.
chunks.checkText: Which type of radiation needs thick lead to block it?

chunks.heading: Measuring atoms against carbon-12
chunks.body: Atoms are far too light to weigh in grams easily. So scientists compare every atom's mass to carbon-12, which is fixed at exactly 12 units.
chunks.checkText: Atomic masses are compared against which isotope?

chunks.heading: One element, one average mass
chunks.body: Most elements are a mix of [[chem-isotopes|isotopes]] with slightly different masses. Relative atomic mass is the average mass of all of them, weighted by how common each one is.
chunks.checkText: Relative atomic mass is a kind of...

checkOptions.text: The mass of the lightest isotope only
A fixed number that's the same for every element

chunks.heading: Weighing atoms with a machine
chunks.body: A mass spectrometer is a machine that separates an element's [[chem-isotopes|isotopes]] and measures the mass and abundance of each one.
chunks.checkText: What does a mass spectrometer measure?

checkOptions.text: The mass and abundance of isotopes

chunks.heading: Flame tests: metals in colour
chunks.body: When a metal is heated in a flame, it glows with its own characteristic colour. This lets chemists identify which metal is present.
chunks.checkText: A flame test helps identify a metal by its...

chunks.heading: The light each element gives off
chunks.body: Passing a heated element's light through a prism splits it into a pattern of coloured lines. Every element produces its own unique pattern, called an emission spectrum.
chunks.checkText: An emission spectrum for an element is...

chunks.heading: Electrons live in shells
chunks.body: Electrons are arranged in shells around the [[chem-atom-structure|nucleus]], numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. Shells closer to the nucleus hold lower-energy electrons.
chunks.checkText: Which shell holds the lowest-energy electrons?

chunks.heading: Why heated atoms glow
chunks.body: Heating an atom can push an electron up to a higher [[chem-electron-shells|shell]]. When it falls back down, it releases the extra energy as light — producing the lines in an [[chem-emission-spectra|emission spectrum]].
chunks.checkText: An electron releases light when it...

checkOptions.text: Falls back to a lower shell

chunks.heading: How many electrons fit in a shell
chunks.body: Each [[chem-electron-shells|shell]] can only hold a set maximum number of electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, 18 in the third.
chunks.checkText: The first electron shell can hold a maximum of...

chunks.heading: Writing an atom's electron arrangement
chunks.body: Electrons fill the lowest [[chem-electron-shells|shell]] first, then the next, until they run out. Writing the count in each shell, like 2,8,1, gives the electron configuration.
chunks.checkText: Electrons fill shells starting from...

checkOptions.text: The shell closest to the nucleus
Whichever shell has space, in any order

chunks.heading: The electrons that matter most
chunks.body: The electrons in an atom's outermost shell are called valence electrons. These are the ones involved when the atom reacts with other atoms.
chunks.checkText: Valence electrons are found in...

chunks.heading: Electrons as clouds, not orbits
chunks.body: The Schrödinger model says electrons don't travel in fixed paths like the earlier [[chem-electron-shells|shell]] model suggested. Instead, they behave like clouds of probability around the nucleus.
chunks.checkText: The Schrödinger model describes electrons as...

checkOptions.text: Cloud-like, not travelling in fixed paths
Tiny balls orbiting in exact circles

chunks.heading: Shells within shells
chunks.body: Each [[chem-electron-shells|shell]] is actually made of smaller subshells, labelled s, p, d and f. Each subshell can hold its own set number of electrons.
chunks.checkText: Subshells are labelled using the letters...

chunks.heading: Filling the lowest energy first
chunks.body: The Aufbau principle says electrons always fill the lowest-energy [[chem-subshells|subshell]] available before moving to a higher one.
chunks.checkText: According to the Aufbau principle, electrons fill...

chunks.heading: Rows and columns of elements
chunks.body: The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing [[chem-atomic-number|atomic number]]. Its rows are called periods and its columns are called groups.
chunks.checkText: Elements in the periodic table are ordered by...

chunks.heading: What a group tells you
chunks.body: Elements in the same group have the same number of [[chem-valence-electrons|valence electrons]]. That's why they tend to react in similar ways.
chunks.checkText: Elements in the same group share the same number of...

chunks.heading: What a period tells you
chunks.body: The period number of an element equals the number of electron [[chem-electron-shells|shells]] its atoms use. Elements in period 3, for example, all use three shells.
chunks.checkText: An element's period number tells you its number of...

chunks.heading: The four blocks of the table
chunks.body: The periodic table has four blocks, named after the type of [[chem-subshells|subshell]] being filled: s, p, d and f. An element's block matches its highest-energy subshell.
chunks.checkText: The blocks of the periodic table are named after...

chunks.heading: The pull felt by outer electrons
chunks.body: Core charge is the pull a [[chem-valence-electrons|valence electron]] feels from the nucleus, after inner-shell electrons shield part of that pull.
chunks.checkText: Core charge measures the pull felt by...

chunks.heading: How strongly an atom attracts electrons
chunks.body: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls electrons towards itself. A higher [[chem-core-charge|core charge]] means a stronger pull, so electronegativity increases across a period.
chunks.checkText: A higher core charge generally means...

chunks.heading: How big is an atom?
chunks.body: Atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outer, valence-shell electrons. It shrinks across a period as [[chem-core-charge|core charge]] pulls those electrons in tighter.
chunks.checkText: Atomic radius tends to decrease across a period because...

checkOptions.text: Core charge increases, pulling electrons closer

chunks.heading: The energy to remove an electron
chunks.body: First ionisation energy is the energy needed to pull one electron off an atom. It generally increases across a period, because [[chem-core-charge|core charge]] holds electrons more tightly.
chunks.checkText: First ionisation energy generally increases...

checkOptions.text: Across a period, left to right
